what_its_for: Valacyclovir is an antiviral medicine used to treat infections caused by certain viruses. It is commonly used to treat cold sores (fever blisters), genital herpes, shingles (herpes zoster), and chickenpox. It helps reduce pain, speed up healing, and lessen the number of outbreaks. It does not cure herpes, but it can help manage symptoms and lower the chance of spreading it to others.
how_to_take: Take valacyclovir by mouth with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water (8 ounces). Drink plenty of fluids while taking this medicine to help protect your kidneys. Take it exactly as your doctor tells you and finish the full course, even if you start feeling better. For cold sores and genital herpes, starting treatment as soon as you notice symptoms (such as tingling, burning, or blisters) works best.
dosing: Your dose depends on what condition is being treated, how severe it is, and how well your kidneys work. Common doses include: Cold sores: 2,000 mg twice a day for 1 day. Genital herpes (first outbreak): 1,000 mg twice a day for 10 days. Genital herpes (repeat outbreaks): 500 mg twice a day for 3 days. Suppression therapy (to reduce outbreaks): 500–1,000 mg once daily. Shingles: 1,000 mg three times a day for 7 days. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as your dose may be different.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store valacyclovir at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it after the expiration date on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid sexual contact when you have any symptoms of herpes such as sores, tingling, or burning, as you can still spread the virus even while taking this medicine. Use a condom every time you have sex to help lower the risk of spreading herpes to others. Avoid letting the medicine touch your eyes. Limit alcohol, as it can cause dehydration and increase side effects. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you take, since some medications like those used for kidney problems (such as cimetidine or probenecid) can interact with valacyclovir.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience: confusion, difficulty speaking, or hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there); extreme weakness or shakiness; decreased urination or no urination at all; signs of a serious kidney problem such as swelling in your legs or ankles; unusual bruising or bleeding; pale or yellowed skin; fast heartbeat; fever. Also call your doctor if your symptoms do not improve, if they get worse, or if you develop new sores or blisters. Serious side effects are rare but can happen, especially in people with weakened immune systems or kidney problems.
when_it_works: Valacyclovir works best when started as soon as possible after symptoms begin. For cold sores and genital herpes outbreaks, you may notice improvement within 2 to 3 days. For shingles, symptoms usually start to improve within a few days of starting treatment. The medicine does not remove the virus from your body, but it does slow down the virus and helps your body heal faster.
special_populations: Older adults: Older people are more likely to have kidney problems, so your doctor may start you on a lower dose. Drink plenty of fluids and report any confusion or changes in urination right away. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Valacyclovir may be used during pregnancy when the benefits outweigh the risks, but your doctor will decide what is safest for you and your baby. Children: Valacyclovir can be used in children for chickenpox and cold sores, but the dose is based on weight. Follow your child's doctor's instructions carefully. Kidney problems: If you have kidney disease, your doctor will lower your dose or change how often you take the medicine to protect your kidneys.
